question.leadin: Name these people who all formulated their own law codes.
question.text: This Babylonian king created a namesake law code that demanded "an eye for an eye."
question.clue: This Amorite king went up a mountain to receive a stele from the sun god Shamash that was later discovered in Susa.

swap.leadin: Answer the following questions about the development of writing.
swap.text: The first known example of writing comes from this system used in ancient Mesopotamia. The name for this writing system derives from the wedges used to carve this writing system into clay tablets.
swap.clue: Henry Rawlinson studied the Behistun Inscription for insight into this system, which is seen on the oldest complaint tablet.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about Mesopotamia's earliest civilization, Sumer.
question.text: Before its ultimate collapse, Sumer experienced a renaissance during the Third Dynasty of this city, which saw the writing of the Epic of Gilgamesh. This city was home to the Great Ziggurat.
question.clue: A king named -Nammu, who founded a dynasty that supplanted Lagash and the Gutians, was succeeded by Shulgi.

swap.leadin: Leonard Woolley unearthed one of these structures constructed of 720,000 mud bricks and dedicated to the Moon Goddess Nanna.
swap.text: Name these stepped temples, a "Great" one of which was built in Ur. Stories of the Tower of Babel may have been inspired by one of these buildings which was dedicated to Marduk.
swap.clue: Koldewey also found one that he took to be a temple to Marduk, the name of which, Etemenanki, translates as "The Foundation of Heaven and Earth."

question.text: This Neo-Assyrian ruler's destructive conquest of Elam is sometimes considered genocide. This ruler's namesake library, discovered by Austen Henry Layard, contained the Epic of Gilgamesh.
question.clue: He had earlier conquered the Elamite capital Susa, and that defeat of the Kushite armies near Memphis allowed him to take the Egyptian capital.

swap.leadin: The language spoken in this empire replaced the Sumerian language and is believed to be the earliest Semitic language.
swap.text: This Mesopotamian empire was the largest in recorded history at the time. It reached its greatest extent under the rule of Naram-Sin.
swap.clue: Its most famous ruler's life was detailed on the Ebla tablets, and started out as a cup-bearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish.

question.leadin: Leaders of the "neo" incarnation of this empire included founder Tiglath-Pileser III, Sennacherib, and a noted library-owner, Ashurbanipal.
question.text: Name this ancient empire of the Fertile Crescent, with capital at Nineveh.
question.clue: The Epic of Gilgamesh was discovered in a library built by one of this empire's monarchs.

swap.text: This Assyrian capital was located on the northern part of the Tigris.
swap.clue: Sennacherib transformed this city, which had massive Lamassu door figures.

question.leadin: For several millennia, sofers have worked in this profession in Jewish communities.
question.text: Identify this profession. People working in this profession in Ancient Egypt would likely have carried out their work using the Demotic script.
question.clue: The god Nabu is often depicted holding equipment central to this profession.

swap.text: Fragments of Hammurabi's Code have been found in this city, whose "scribal corner" is rich with ancient texts. Various Mesopotamian dynasties sought to control this city of religious importance, the home of the god Enlil.
swap.clue: The best example of a Sumerian schoolhouse was found in this city, which was the center of worship for Enlil. This city's Ekur Temple was rebuilt by Naram-Sin.

question.text: This warrior king from the north invaded Sumer beginning around 2340 BCE, creating a unified empire there for the first time.
question.clue: After taking Kish from Lugulzaggesi, he built his empire by extending trade from his capital city throughout to Susa and the Zagros mountains.

swap.leadin: The oldest surviving hymn in the world was written in the language of this civilization.
swap.text: Name this Hurrian kingdom and rival of the Hittites governed from Wassukani. Its king Tusratta wrote a letter to Akhenaten about "The Missing Gold Statues Again."
swap.clue: Based on terms in the Kikkuli horse-training manual, the names of several rulers, and a list of deities found in a treaty, the rulers of this polity are argued to have been Indo-Europeans.

question.text: This Sumerian city, which the ancients considered the world's oldest, contained Enki's cult center, the E-Abzu or "House of Deep Waters." Silt accumulated in the Persian Gulf south of this city, where Amar-Sin built a ziggurat.
question.answerHtml: Eridu [or Irîtu; accept Tell Abu Shahrain; accept Eridu Genesis] (Eridu was once located on the sea, but the silt eventually shifted it over 100 miles inland.)
question.clue: This Mesopotamian city whose rulers are the first kings mentioned on the Sumerian King List, which is often taken as evidence for this city being the oldest in Sumerian civilization.

swap.leadin: In one tomb, this archaeologist discovered a headdress made of golden leaves, four stringed lyres, and a golden and lapis lazuli encrusted bull's head.
swap.text: Name this British archaeologist who in 1922 led an excavation of the Sumerian city of Ur.
swap.clue: This archaeologist made a name for himself by discovering the Great Ziggurat and other buildings at Ur, a Sumerian city then thought to be the world's oldest.

question.text: This ethnic group largely made up the population of the Mitanni Kingdom to the southeast of the Hittite Empire. Kikkuli ("kee-KOO-lee") wrote a horse training manual in this ethnic group's namesake language, which was most closely related to Urartian.
question.answerHtml: Hurrians [or Khurrites or Hourri or Hurriter or Hari; accept Hurrian language; accept Hurro-Urartian languages]
question.clue: This people whose namesake language was primarily spoken in the Mitanni kingdom.

swap.leadin: This ruler is the main character of the Cutha Legend and The Great Revolt, which may have inspired later legends to blame him for Akkad's conquest by the Gutians.
swap.text: Name this ruler of the Akkadian Empire during its territorial peak and the first to proclaim his own divinity. This ruler's namesake "Victory Stele" depicts his victory over the Lullubi people.
swap.clue: This king who ruled during the height of the Akkadian Empire, and erected a notable victory stele boasting of his defeat of the mountain people of Lullubi and depicting himself as a god.

question.text: Several Chaldaean leaders, including Marduk-apla-usur and Eriba-Marduk, ruled over this kingdom in the 8th century B.C. Nebuchadnezzar II ruled during the "Chaldean dynasty" of a "Neo-" empire of this kingdom.
question.clue: A raid from its western neighbors left it in the hands of the Kassites, and part of it was destroyed by Sennacherib but later rebuilt by his son Essarhadon.

swap.text: One of the languages in Darius the Great's Behistun Inscription was the language of these people, based at Susa. Their Old Kingdom was conquered by Shulgi of Ur, although they rebounded under Kutir-Nahhunte I.
swap.clue: Another ruler of this kingdom installed his son Warad-Sin on the throne of Larsa.

question.text: The Akkadian dynasty was founded by Sargon, who rose to prominence as cupbearer to Urzababa, the king of this city. Just east of Babylon, this was the traditional first capital of Sumeria after the "Great Flood" and the king of its first dynasty is recorded as Jushur.
question.clue: Kugbau, the grandmother of a famous ruler of this city and one-time alewife, is the first known woman to rule in her own name in Mesopotamia.

swap.leadin: This kingdom's capital was Washukanni. FTPE.
swap.text: Name this Ancient Near Eastern Empire, noted for its rivalry with the Hittites, Assyrians, and Egyptians.
swap.clue: Thutmose IV proposed seven times to marry a princess of this polity, and some scholars have identified Nefertiti with a princess of this polity named Tadukhipa.
